claims.claim: Eustathius was a native of Side in Pamphylia.
He was bishop of Beroea around 320 before becoming patriarch of Antioch shortly before the Council of Nicaea in 325.
He was one of the most prominent opponents of Arianism at the Council of Nicaea and engaged in almost continuous literary warfare against the Arians from 325-330.
He was deposed by a synod at Antioch in 330 for Sabellianism, confirmed by the emperor, and banished to Trajanopolis in Thrace.
The work De fide contra Arianos was written out of love for the catholic faith and was initially given to a friend to read, who then had it transcribed.
The author requested that the work be circulated anonymously at first to learned and prudent men so that it could be emended by the counsel of many if anything seemed excessive or deficient.
The controversy concerned the Arian claim that the Son of God was mutable and convertible, not from the Father's own substance, with a temporal beginning and birth from nothing.
It is listed as CPG 3358 in the Clavis Patrum Graecorum and was edited by J.H. Declerck in the modern critical edition of Eustathius's complete works.
Eustathius and Marcellus joined forces with Alexander of Alexandria at Nicaea and significantly influenced the formulation of the Nicene Creed.
